name: Ambiguity Bias
description: Given a choice, people often prefer options with known odds over comparable options whose probabilities are unclear or hard to estimate. Uncertainty about the distribution itself feels aversive, not just uncertainty about the outcome.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to pricing/comparison tables, privacy and warranty disclosures, novel AI features, and any UI asking users to choose under uncertainty: clearer odds, bounds, and guarantees often beat vaguer but potentially better options.
prevalence_note: Common in behavioral economics, finance, and risk-decision writing, but usually implicit rather than explicitly named in everyday product-design discourse.

findings.description: A representative US household survey measuring ambiguity aversion via Ellsberg-urn-based questions found it directly predicts five real financial-decision puzzles: lower stock-market participation, lower equity allocation, more home-bias, more own-company stock ownership, and (conditional on owning stocks) more portfolio under-diversification. Ambiguity-averse respondents were also more likely to sell stocks during the financial crisis. A genuine, real-world, high-stakes demonstration that ambiguity aversion is not just a lab artifact but predicts consequential financial behavior.
findings.source_title: Ambiguity aversion and household portfolio choice puzzles: Empirical evidence

findings.description: In a series of studies, people preferred prospects with known probabilities over ambiguous ones in comparative settings, but this ambiguity aversion seemed to disappear when a vague prospect was evaluated in isolation rather than alongside a clearer alternative.
